questions.question_text: Which description gives the correct sketch of $y=(x-3)^{2}(x+3)$?

options.text: It cuts the axis at $(-3,0)$, has a maximum at $(-1,32)$ and touches the axis at the minimum $(3,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
It cuts the axis at $(-3,0)$, has a minimum at $(-1,32)$ and touches the axis at the maximum $(3,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Swapped the stationary-point natures: $P''(-1)=-12<0$ gives a maximum and $P''(3)=12>0$ gives a minimum.

options.text: It cuts the axis at $(-3,0)$, has a maximum at $(-1,-32)$ and touches the axis at the minimum $(3,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Changed the sign when evaluating $P(-1)=(-4)^{2}(2)=32$.

options.text: It cuts the axis at $(3,0)$, has a minimum at $(1,-32)$ and touches the axis at the maximum $(-3,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Reversed the factor signs, sketching $y=(x+3)^{2}(x-3)$ instead.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-3$ is a simple zero and $x=3$ is a double zero, so the curve cuts at $(-3,0)$ and touches at $(3,0)$.
$P(0)=27$
$P(x)=x^{3}-3x^{2}-9x+27$
$P'(x)=3x^{2}-6x-9=3(x-3)(x+1)$
$x=3$ or $x=-1$
$P(-1)=32$, $P(3)=0$
$P''(x)=6x-6$
$P''(-1)=-12<0$, so $(-1,32)$ is a maximum.
$P''(3)=12>0$, so $(3,0)$ is a minimum.
The leading term is $x^{3}$, so the left end falls and the right end rises.

questions.question_text: Which description gives the correct sketch of $y=x(x+3)^{2}$?

options.text: It touches the axis at the maximum $(-3,0)$, has a minimum at $(-1,-4)$ and cuts the axis at $(0,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
It cuts the axis at $(-3,0)$, has a minimum at $(-1,-4)$ and touches the axis at $(0,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Assigned the repeated zero to the factor $x$ instead of $(x+3)^{2}$, reversing the behaviour at the two intercepts.

options.text: It touches the axis at the maximum $(3,0)$, has a minimum at $(1,-4)$ and cuts the axis at $(0,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Reversed the signs of the stationary-point abscissae; solving $P'(x)=3(x+1)(x+3)=0$ gives $x=-1$ and $x=-3$.

options.text: It touches the axis at the maximum $(-3,0)$, has a minimum at $(-1,4)$ and cuts the axis at $(0,0)$; its left end falls and its right end rises.
options.why: Lost the negative factor when evaluating $P(-1)=(-1)(2)^{2}=-4$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-3$ is a double zero and $x=0$ is a simple zero.
$P(x)=x^{3}+6x^{2}+9x$
$P'(x)=3x^{2}+12x+9=3(x+1)(x+3)$
$x=-3$ or $x=-1$
$P(-3)=0$, $P(-1)=-4$
$P''(x)=6x+12$
$P''(-3)=-6<0$, so $(-3,0)$ is a maximum.
$P''(-1)=6>0$, so $(-1,-4)$ is a minimum.
The sketch touches the axis at $(-3,0)$ and cuts it at $(0,0)$, which is also the $y$-intercept.
The leading term is $x^{3}$, so the left end falls and the right end rises.

questions.question_text: Which statement about the graph of $y=(x-1)^{2}(x+3)^{2}$ is correct?

options.text: It touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,16)$.
It touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,4)$.
options.why: Evaluated only one bracket at $x=-1$; the full value is $P(-1)=(-2)^{2}(2)^{2}=4\times4=16$, not $4$.

options.text: It cuts the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,16)$.
options.why: Read each zero as multiplicity $1$; both zeroes have multiplicity $2$, so the curve touches the axis and turns back rather than crossing.

options.text: It cuts the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$ and $(-3,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,4)$.
options.why: Both slips together: the zeroes read as simple, and only one bracket evaluated at $x=-1$.

questions.solution_text:
$P(x)=\left(x^{2}+2x-3\right)^{2}$
$P'(x)=2\left(x^{2}+2x-3\right)(2x+2)$
$x=1$, $x=-3$ or $x=-1$
$P(1)=0$
$P(-3)=0$
$P(-1)=(-2)^{2}(2)^{2}$
$=4\times4$
$=16$
Both zeroes have multiplicity $2$, so they are minimums on the axis, and $(-1,16)$ between them is a maximum.

questions.question_text: Which description gives the correct sketch of $y=-2(x+2)^{3}(x-2)$?

options.text: Both ends fall; the curve crosses at the horizontal inflection $(-2,0)$, rises to a maximum at $(1,54)$ and cuts the axis at $(2,0)$.
Both ends rise; the curve crosses at the horizontal inflection $(-2,0)$, falls to a minimum at $(1,-54)$ and cuts the axis at $(2,0)$.
options.why: Omitted the negative sign in the coefficient, sketching $y=2(x+2)^{3}(x-2)$ instead.

options.text: Both ends fall; the curve touches the axis at the maximum $(-2,0)$, rises to a maximum at $(1,54)$ and cuts the axis at $(2,0)$.
options.why: Treated the triple zero as an even-multiplicity zero; it is a horizontal inflection where the curve crosses.

options.text: Both ends fall; the curve crosses at the horizontal inflection $(-2,0)$, rises to a maximum at $(1,27)$ and cuts the axis at $(2,0)$.
options.why: Omitted the coefficient $2$ when calculating the maximum value: $P(1)=-2(3)^{3}(-1)=54$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-2$ has multiplicity $3$, so the curve crosses at a horizontal inflection; $x=2$ is a simple zero, so the curve cuts the axis there.
$P(0)=32$
$P'(x)=-2[3(x+2)^{2}(x-2)+(x+2)^{3}]$
$=-8(x+2)^{2}(x-1)$
$x=-2$ or $x=1$
$P'$ remains positive on either side of $x=-2$, so $(-2,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection.
$P'$ changes from positive to negative at $x=1$, so $(1,54)$ is a maximum.
The leading term is $-2x^{4}$, so both ends fall.

questions.question_text: Which description gives the correct sketch of $y=(x-3)^{3}(x+1)$?

options.text: Both ends rise; the curve cuts the axis at $(-1,0)$, falls to a minimum at $(0,-27)$ and crosses at the horizontal inflection $(3,0)$.
Both ends rise; the curve cuts the axis at $(-1,0)$, falls to a minimum at $(0,-27)$ and touches the axis at a minimum at $(3,0)$.
options.why: Treated the triple zero as an even-multiplicity zero; at $x=3$ the curve crosses at a horizontal inflection.

options.text: Both ends rise; the curve cuts the axis at $(-1,0)$, has a maximum at $(0,-27)$ and crosses at the horizontal inflection $(3,0)$.
options.why: Reversed the derivative sign change at $x=0$: $P'$ changes from negative to positive, giving a minimum.

options.text: Both ends rise; the curve cuts the axis at $(-1,0)$, falls to a minimum at $(0,-9)$ and crosses at the horizontal inflection $(3,0)$.
options.why: Squared the magnitude $3$ while retaining the negative sign, producing $-3^{2}=-9$ instead of $(-3)^{3}=-27$ when evaluating $P(0)$.

questions.solution_text:
$x=-1$ is a simple zero and $x=3$ is a triple zero.
$P(0)=-27$
$P'(x)=3(x-3)^{2}(x+1)+(x-3)^{3}$
$=(x-3)^{2}(3x+3+x-3)=4x(x-3)^{2}$
$x=0$ or $x=3$
$P'$ changes from negative to positive at $x=0$, so $(0,-27)$ is a minimum.
$P'$ remains positive on either side of $x=3$, so $(3,0)$ is a horizontal point of inflection where the curve crosses.
The leading term is $x^{4}$, so both ends rise.

questions.question_text: Which description gives the correct sketch of $y=x^{2}(x+2)^{2}$?

options.text: Both ends rise; the curve touches the axis at the minimums $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,1)$ between them.
Both ends rise; the curve cuts the axis at $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,1)$ between them.
options.why: Ignored the even multiplicities; both zeroes are double zeroes, so the curve touches rather than crosses.

options.text: Both ends rise; the curve touches the axis at the minimums $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$, with a maximum at $(-1,4)$ between them.
options.why: Used the intercept separation squared instead of evaluating $P(-1)=(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}=1$.

options.text: Both ends fall; the curve touches the axis at the maximums $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$, with a minimum at $(-1,-1)$ between them.
options.why: Inserted a negative leading coefficient, sketching $y=-x^{2}(x+2)^{2}$ instead.

questions.solution_text:
Both zeroes, $x=-2$ and $x=0$, have multiplicity $2$, so the curve touches the axis at each.
$P(x)=x^{4}+4x^{3}+4x^{2}$
$P'(x)=4x^{3}+12x^{2}+8x=4x(x+1)(x+2)$
$x=-2$, $x=-1$ or $x=0$
$P(-2)=0$, $P(-1)=1$, $P(0)=0$
$P''(x)=12x^{2}+24x+8$
$P''(-2)=P''(0)=8>0$, so $(-2,0)$ and $(0,0)$ are minimums.
$P''(-1)=-4<0$, so $(-1,1)$ is a maximum.
The leading term is $x^{4}$, so both ends rise.

questions.question_text:
A cubic curve touches the $x$-axis at $x=-3$, cuts it at $x=2$, and has $y$-intercept $-18$.
What is its equation, and what is the nature of the stationary point at $x=-3$?

options.text: $y=(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$, with a maximum at $(-3,0)$
$y=(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$, with a minimum at $(-3,0)$
options.why: The curve rises to the axis and falls away again to the right, so $(-3,0)$ is a maximum; $P''(-3)=-10<0$.

options.text: $y=(x-3)^{2}(x+2)$, with a maximum at $(3,0)$
options.why: The signs inside the brackets are reversed, giving intercepts at $3$ and $-2$; the classification is also incorrect because for this polynomial $P''(3)=10>0$, so $(3,0)$ is a minimum.

options.text: $y=-(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$, with a minimum at $(-3,0)$
options.why: Sign error in $k$: $y=k(9)(-2)=-18k=-18$ gives $k=1$, not $-1$.

questions.solution_text:
Touching at $x=-3$ needs an even multiplicity, so $(x+3)^{2}$ is a factor.
$y=k(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$
$-18=k(3)^{2}(-2)$
$-18=-18k$
$k=1$
$y=(x+3)^{2}(x-2)$
$P(x)=x^{3}+4x^{2}-3x-18$
$P''(x)=6x+8$
$P''(-3)=-10<0$, so $(-3,0)$ is a maximum.

\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$x$}, ylabel={$y$}, xmin=-5.3, xmax=3.2, ymin=-25.5, ymax=25.5, samples=120, clip=false, width=9cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[smooth, thick, <->, domain=-4.9:2.76] {(x+3)*(x+3)*(x-2)};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
